C90B Electrical System Overview
The aircraft electrical system is a twenty eight volt direct current system, designed for reliability, redundancy, and automatic protection.
Power comes from two main sources.
A battery, used for engine starts and backup power,
and two starter generators, which provide primary power during flight.
The battery is always connected to the hot battery bus.
This means some systems can receive power even when the battery switch is off.
Use caution to avoid draining the battery.
Each engine has a starter generator.
During engine start, it acts as a starter.
Once the engine is running, it becomes a generator and supplies electrical power.
Each generator can produce up to two hundred fifty amps,
and normally maintains about twenty eight volts.
The system uses multiple electrical buses.
These include the left generator bus,
right generator bus,
center bus,
triple fed bus,
and the battery bus.
The key idea is redundancy.
Critical systems are connected to more than one power source,
so if one part fails, others can continue supplying power.
In normal operation, all buses are connected together automatically.
Both generators share the electrical load,
power the entire aircraft,
and keep the battery charged.
The system includes automatic protection features.
One of the most important is the bus tie system.
Sensors monitor current flow.
If a high current is detected, indicating a fault,
the system isolates that part of the electrical system.
This prevents the fault from affecting the rest of the aircraft.
Current limiters provide additional protection,
acting like slow blow fuses.
Another key feature is load shedding.
If both generators fail,
the system automatically removes non essential electrical loads.
The battery will then power only critical buses.
In this situation,
land as soon as practical.
There are manual controls for the bus tie system.
The bus sense switch allows testing or resetting after a fault.
The generator ties switch allows manual control of generator connections.
A fault must be reset before ties can be reconnected.
The battery system may include a charge monitor.
A high charge rate after engine start is normal,
and will decrease as the battery recharges.
Each generator is controlled by a generator control unit.
This unit regulates voltage,
protects against overvoltage,
prevents reverse current,
and balances load between generators.
For engine starts,
the first engine is started using the battery.
The second engine uses a cross start,
drawing power from the battery and the operating generator.
During starts,
some protection systems are temporarily bypassed.
The aircraft uses inverters to supply alternating current power.
Two inverters are installed,
and either one can power the system.
If one source fails,
another is automatically used.
External power can be used on the ground.
The battery must be connected first.
Voltage and polarity must be correct.
Circuit breakers protect individual systems.
If a non essential breaker trips in flight,
do not reset it.
If an essential breaker trips,
wait thirty seconds and reset it once.
If it trips again,
leave it out.
Overall,
the system is highly automated and designed to protect itself.
Most failures isolate automatically.
The most critical situation is loss of both generators.
In that case,
reduce electrical load,
and land as soon as practical.
